paras: The assault on Charles Collins was an attack by two white men on Collins, a Black saloon porter, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, on the night of 8 August 1903. Collins was badly bruised, and the attackers were not identified. The Saint Paul Globe reported it as one of several recent attacks on Black men in the city, which had prompted police orders to stop what its headline called a "race war."

According to the Globe, Minneapolis had seen "several more or less aggravated instances" of "demonstrations against colored men" in the days before the assault. On the Thursday night before, several white men had attacked two Black men eating ice cream in a candy store at Third Street and First Avenue, until a police officer stopped the fight. Police traced the trouble to a recent feud between "a certain class of whites" and Black workers kept downtown at night.

Collins, described as "a St. Paul colored man," worked as porter in a saloon at Washington and Hennepin. On the night of 8 August two unknown white men assaulted him and left him badly bruised. Collins carried a knife, but his white wife clung about his neck and was "largely instrumental" in keeping him from using it.

No arrest in the Collins case appears in the coverage. Police were told to "immediately and forcibly suppress" such demonstrations, and Superintendent Conroy ordered the arrest of anyone, of any color, who caused a street disturbance. Black men married to white women, the Globe reported, were "much excited" and held several meetings to decide how they would act if attacked.

The only account found, in either press, ran on page 5 of the Saint Paul Globe on 9 August 1903, in its Minneapolis column under the headline "Police Get Orders to Stop Race War." The Globe gave much of the piece to white wives of Black men, quoting one of Swedish parentage who called Black Minnesotans "well behaved and hard working" and blamed "a few drunken rowdies." It closed on the department's resolve to suppress "negro baiting."

accounts.label: Saint Paul Globe Minneapolis column
accounts.gist: Two unknown white men assaulted and badly bruised Collins; a 'cutting affray' was averted because his white wife held him back from using his knife. The paper presented it as one of several recent attacks on colored men, especially those married to white women.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Police Get Orders to Stop Race War' and 'Prompt Arrests Will Follow Further Negro Beating'; printed a white wife's defense of her husband and of Black men as 'well behaved and hard working' and reported police resolve to suppress 'negro baiting'.

sources.note: Minneapolis column, 'Police Get Orders to Stop Race War': Collins beaten 'last night' by two unknown white men; also a Thursday-night assault on two colored men; police orders; interviews with white wives of Black men.
quotes: Last night Charles Collins, a St. Paul colored man employed as porter in a saloon at Washington and Hennepin, was assaulted by two unknown white men and badly bruised.
There would have been a cutting affray but for the white wife of the assaulted man, who clung about his neck and was largely instrumental in preventing his use of the knife he carried.
The police of Minneapolis are under instructions to immediately and forcibly suppress demonstrations against colored men
The department is determined to suppress any tendency toward negro baiting in Minneapolis and persons suspected of such tendencies are being closely watched.
